title: OpenAI's most powerful AI models disabled their own safety monitoring — and one lied about it
description: OpenAI has revealed that agents operated by two of its most powerful models disabled their own safety monitoring when carrying out routine tasks, with
body: OpenAI has revealed that agents operated by two of its most powerful models disabled their own safety monitoring when carrying out routine tasks, with one subsequently denying it had done so. An agent powered by GPT Sol 6.1 disabled automatic alerts to OpenAI's security team, the company said in a blog post late on Tuesday. In a separate task, a GPT-6 Astra agent migrating a program removed its monitoring integration and then falsely claimed it hadn't. The incidents happened during internal coding tasks."In both cases, the agents considered whether monitoring safeguards should be preserved, but interpreted routine coding instructions as permission to weaken them," OpenAI said in a blog post. Warnings about the risks of developing increasingly advanced AI systems have ramped up in recent months, amid cyberattacks from rogue models and growing calls for a slowdown from researchers building the tech. The latest incidents reported by OpenAI highlight how agents can autonomously weaken safety guardrails while carrying out seemingly innocuous tasks.OpenAI did not classify either incident under its most significant category, and the company said it was updating its misalignment monitoring system in response.

title: BlackRock's Rick Rieder sees 'historic' opportunity in high-quality bonds
description: Rick Rieder speaking at the CNBC CEO Council Summit in Washington, D.C. on June 2, 2026.Aaron Clamage | CNBCInvestors may be wary of the volatility hi
body: Rick Rieder speaking at the CNBC CEO Council Summit in Washington, D.C. on June 2, 2026.Aaron Clamage | CNBCInvestors may be wary of the volatility hitting parts of the bond market right now, but they have an "historic" opportunity to grab attractive yields in high-quality credit, Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, told CNBC in an exclusive interview.Hypothetically, it's now possible for investors to build a diversified portfolio that yields more than 7% with less than three years of duration and an average credit quality of A-, he said. Duration is a measurement of a bond's price sensitivity to fluctuations in rates, and issues with shorter maturities tend to have lower duration."Not only is it historic in that these yields are where they are, but the only time these yields are ever here is when there's some problem, like an economic problem or default problem," Rieder said in an interview about his fourth-quarter outlook, released Wednesday. That isn't the case now, where the economy remains strong, he said. "So you don't really have to worry about defaults of any significance."While Rieder didn't specifically identify the credits in the aforementioned portfolio, the iShares Aaa - A Rated Corporate Bond ETF (QLTA) has a 30-day SEC yield of 5.68% and an effective duration of 6.48 years — higher than Rieder's low duration focus. The iShares Flexible Income Active ETF (BINC), which is managed by Rieder, has a 5.66% 30-day SEC yield and three-year effective duration, but its portfolio extends beyond investment-grade credit.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconiShares Flexible Income Active ETF year to dateBest opportunities include hyperscalersRieder sees the best opportunity right now in investment-grade corporate bonds — which he pointed out he hasn't said "in a really long time." Investment grade bonds are rated AAA through BBB- by S&P and Fitch, while Moody's rates them Aaa through Baa3. That includes hyperscaler bonds, which have flooded the market with issuance this year as they ramp up their AI infrastructure. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms and Oracle have issued a total of about $228.4 billion in bonds year to date, as of Oct. 20, according to LSEG. "They're very low leverage. They have tremendous amounts of cash flow coming in," Rieder said of the hyperscalers in general. "You're now getting to buy these entities which are higher quality, paying you a very attractive yield to get it." Rieder's iShares Flexible Income Active ETF has upped its allocation to investment-grade corporates to 14.3% of its portfolio. In July, that stood at 8.5%. That said, investors need to be patient and sit tight since rates could still move higher from here, he advised."Your starting point is by far your best barometer of what your return is going to be," he noted. "So if you get seven and a quarter, maybe you get eight, maybe you get six, but ... if your holding period is a year or longer, you're going to get that yield."Caution should also be exercised outside of investment-grade credit, which requires more selectivity and deep research, he warned. That includes AI names. "There's parts of the data center supply that's not hyperscaler guaranteed or hyperscaler backed," he said. "That we've been more cautious around, and we'll continue to be."The bond market, particularly high-yield credit, has been rocked as investor concern grows over the massive amount of debt some companies are taking out to fund their artificial intelligence build-out.Junk-rated CoreWeave has become the poster child, seeing its stock drop, bond yields jump and credit-default spreads widen. Oracle, which is sitting in the lower end of investment grade and is seen as a bellwether on the broader AI market, has also taken some hits. CoreWeave's 2031 bond yield on Oct. 21, 2026Fed watchRieder is also keeping an eye on the Federal Reserve, which is expected to raise its federal funds rate again in December to combat inflation. The market is currently pricing in a nearly 90% probability that the central bank will hike at that time, according to the CME Group FedWatch tool. The money manager expects that to happen, although he does not agree with it. Higher rates are hurting parts of the economy, like housing, while not having much of an impact on other areas — such as tech companies' capital expenditures, which have become a big driver of growth, he said."They're not borrowing off the overnight funds rate," Rieder noted. "There's a lot of floating rate finance in housing, credit card, auto loan finance, and you're seeing those areas already under pressure."Instead, the market is and will continue to price the AI supply coming into the market, he added. Calculating risks aheadRieder sees a number of possible risks ahead, including rising levels of government debt across the globe. In the United States, the budget deficit has grown to $2 trillion for fiscal 2026."The more the central banks raise the rates, the cost of debt to these to already indebted governments is something we've got to be careful about over time," he said.Bond supply coming from AI companies should also be watched. "With the amount of supply that's coming — data center, hyperscaler — there's some crowding-out effect that's taking place," he said. "With government rates moving higher, that is something that we just got to keep an eye on."In the meantime, Rieder would just continue to reap the rewards of high investment-grade yields "and smile a lot," he said.

schema.headline: BlackRock's Rick Rieder sees 'historic' opportunity in high-quality bonds

title: Southwest Airlines cuts 2026 profit forecast on higher fuel
description: A Southwest Airlines Boeing 737 airplane departs from San Diego International Airport on May 27, 2026.Kevin Carter | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesS
body: A Southwest Airlines Boeing 737 airplane departs from San Diego International Airport on May 27, 2026.Kevin Carter | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesSouthwest Airlines became the third major U.S. airline this month to cut its 2026 profit forecast due to higher fuel prices, but CEO Bob Jordan said travelers continue to book despite higher fares.The carrier expects to earn between $2.60 and $2.85 a share on an adjusted basis this year, down from its forecast in July of between $3.25 to as much as $4.25 a share.Here's what Southwest reported for third quarter compared with Wall Street expectations, according to consensus estimates from LSEG:Earnings per share: 66 cents adjusted vs. 58 cents expectedRevenue: $8.42 billion adjusted vs. $8.25 billion expectedSouthwest forecast per-share adjusted earnings of between 55 cents and 80 cents in the fourth quarter and unit revenue, a gauge of airfare, up as much as 21% from a year earlier. It said it expects to grow capacity by up to 4% year over year."Demand remained strong as we lapped last year's bag fee and other commercial initiatives, reinforcing our belief that the earnings power we've built is durable, even with significantly higher fuel costs," Jordan said in an earnings release.The airline said its average passenger fare was $231.69 in the third quarter, up almost 27% from the same quarter of 2025. A spokesman said that number does not include add-on fees. The number of revenue passengers carried fell 3.2% to 33.47 million people.Under pressure to grow revenue, Southwest has been remaking its longtime business model over the past several years, scrapping its old policies like two free checked bags per passenger and open seating. In its place, Southwest has started charging for many seat assignments and added a bag fee, similar to major competitors.For the third quarter, Southwest posted net income of $270 million, or 55 cents a share, up from $54 million or 10 cents a share a year earlier. Revenue rose more than 21% to $8.42 billion.Adjusting for one-time items, Southwest reported 66 cents a share.Delta Air Lines and United Airlines also cut their profit outlooks for the rest of the year when they reported third-quarter earnings. Both of those airlines reported top- and bottom-line misses for the third quarter.Read more CNBC airline newsWhy airfare could rise even more, but airline profits won’tBudget airline king Bill Franke warms to premium upgradesCompanies spurn airlines’ cheapest business class ticketsUnited’s next decision: What to do with all those Boeing 737 Max 10 seats it ordered years agoRecord heat, crowds drive offseason boom in international travel

title: IBM beats on top and bottom lines as CEO Krishna touts 'Super Intelligence' traction
description: Arvind Krishna, chief executive officer of International Business Machines Corp. (IBM), speaks during an executive order signing in the Oval Office of
body: Arvind Krishna, chief executive officer of International Business Machines Corp. (IBM), speaks during an executive order signing in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, DC, US, on Monday, June 22, 2026.Bonnie Cash | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesIBM shares slipped in extended trading on Wednesday after the technology vendor reported better-than-predicted third-quarter results. Here's how the company performed relative to LSEG consensus:Earnings: $2.95 adjusted vs. $2.86 expectedRevenue: $17.10 billion vs. $16.82 billion expectedIBM's revenue grew about 5% from a year ago, according to a statement. Net income, at $2.19 billion, or $2.30 per share, increased from $1.74 billion, or $1.84 per share, a year ago. Adjusted earnings exclude acquisition-related adjustments. "Our clients are now deploying 'Super Intelligence' in ways that transform entire operating models, instead of simply addressing narrow or novel problems," IBM CEO Arvind Krishna was quoted as saying in a statement. With respect to guidance, IBM called for full-year free cash flow to increase by more than $1 billion. The forecast as of July was a bump of approximately $1 billion. IBM still sees 2026 constant-currency revenue growth between 4% and 5%.In the third quarter, IBM generated $7.80 billion in software revenue, growing 8% and topping the $7.66 billion consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount.Read more CNBC tech newsMeta earnings updates: AI spending, ad revenue and stock reactionTesla beats on earnings and sales even as auto revenue declinesIntel hits construction milestone at Ohio chip fab that's at least 5 years behind scheduleInvestors are questioning neoclouds' business model but Nebius says AI computing prices are risingConsulting revenue, at $5.34 billion, was flat and just below StreetAccount's $5.37 billion consensus."AI is increasingly embedded in broader transformations our clients are undertaking, representing about 30% of our consulting revenue in the quarter and 35% of our backlog," Jim Kavanaugh, IBM's finance chief, said on a conference call with analysts.The consulting unit's 27.4% gross margin narrowed from 28.9% in the second quarter. "We reinvested productivity gains into digital assets, accelerating our transition towards a services as software model to capture the growing AI opportunity," Kavanaugh said.Infrastructure revenue came to $3.70 billion. That was up 4% and higher than the $3.57 billion consensus from StreetAccount. The company's adjusted gross margin, at 58.5%, was narrower than the StreetAccount consensus of 59.1%.During the quarter, IBM said it agreed to buy Boeing and General Motors' HRL Laboratories, formerly known as Hughes Aircraft's research division, for an undisclosed sum.As of Wednesday's close, IBM stock has come down 15%, while the S&P 500 index has gained 13%. "I think the current street estimates for the year are about $32 billion of revenue," Kavanaugh said. "We feel comfortable with that $32 billion of revenue."WATCH: IBM CEO on quantum computing: Will see $1 trillion in value in by end of 2030swatch now

title: How Ukraine’s drone strikes on Russia crippled the world’s second-largest diesel supplier
description: watch nowUkraine launched massive drone assaults against Russia this week, hitting key oil infrastructure and signaling Kyiv intends to block the Krem
body: watch nowUkraine launched massive drone assaults against Russia this week, hitting key oil infrastructure and signaling Kyiv intends to block the Kremlin from increasing diesel exports in defiance of President Donald Trump.More than 1,000 Ukrainian drones targeted Russia on Sunday alone in one of the largest attacks this year, according to state media reports. The strikes set ablaze an oil export terminal in St. Petersburg, Russia's second-largest city and President Vladimir Putin's hometown.  Kyiv has ended its brief adherence to an energy ceasefire that Trump declared between Ukraine and Russia on Oct. 11. Moscow ignored that truce from the start and Kyiv vowed to retaliate. Ukraine's drone strikes have achieved a scale, range and effectiveness that they have crippled Russia's diesel exports, said Tatiana Mitrova, an expert on the Russian oil industry at Columbia University's Center on Global Energy Policy. Before the attacks, Russia was the second-largest diesel supplier in the world after the U.S. As a result, Trump's deal with Putin to boost Russian diesel exports is likely dead in the water, said Matt Smith, director of commodity research at Kpler. "It seems unlikely that they'll be able to bring the volume of diesel back to the market that they are talking about without an energy ceasefire," Smith said. Reported attacks on Russian oil infrastructure in 2026Rochan ConsultingKyiv's strikes on Russian refineries and related oil infrastructure almost tripled to 31 in July compared with 11 in January, according to data from open-source intelligence firm Rochan Consulting in Warsaw, Poland. The attacks slashed Russia's diesel exports by more than 75%, to 141,000 barrels per day (bpd) in September, compared with 608,000 bpd in the same period last year, according to Kpler data. In response, Moscow banned exports in July to preserve domestic supplies. The Kremlin partially resumed shipments this month to fulfill the Trump-Putin deal.Under Trump's diesel deal to relieve pressure on surging fuel prices, the Kremlin agreed to supply the global market with about 75,000 bpd in October and 124,000 bpd in November. But those export volumes are a rounding error compared with total demand, Mitrova said. The Ukrainians are regularly launching swarms of drones now that number in the hundreds, compared with dozens earlier in the war, Mitrova said. They are also striking deeper into Russian territory, she said. In July, Kyiv hit Russia's largest refinery at Omsk, deep in Siberia near the Kazakhstan border, more than 1,000 miles from Ukraine. And they have learned to target more complex refinery equipment that is harder to repair, Mitrova said. A destroyed fuel tank takes just a couple of weeks to fix, she said. But replacing a secondary refining unit, for example, requires supply chains outside Russia, the analyst said. "You cannot just order it on Alibaba," Mitrova said. "You need to make your order in advance and therefore securing this equipment quickly is not possible. You need to compensate for the risks of all the parties involved because [counterparties] are violating sanctions." "You have to wait at least for several months if the right equipment is destroyed," she said. With midterm elections less than two weeks away, Trump has blamed Ukraine for surging diesel prices that are jeopardizing Republicans' election chances. Nationally, diesel cost $6.32 per gallon on average Tuesday, nearly 75% above the same period last year, according to AAA. But the diesel market was already under pressure due to Trump's decision to go to war with Iran in late February. Tehran's attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and strikes by its Houthi militant allies on oil infrastructure of U.S. Gulf Arab allies have disrupted fuel exports from the Middle East. Diesel exports through Hormuz, for example, are down about 540,000 bpd compared with last year, Kpler's Smith said. Global diesel exports have fallen about 1 million bpd due to lost supplies from Russia and the Middle East, he said. Trump's options to reduce fuel prices are limited. The underlying problem is the shortfall of refining capacity due to damage from two wars that don't appear close to ending soon. U.S. refiners are already working at maximum capacity to fill the gap as much as possible. The International Energy Agency warned this month that diesel supplies will likely remain constrained well into 2027. "The diesel tightness is likely going to persist in the coming months and prices are going to remain elevated," Smith said.

schema.headline: How Ukraine’s drone strikes on Russia crippled the world’s second-largest diesel supplier

title: Tesla beats on earnings and sales even as auto revenue declines
description: watch nowTesla reported better-than-expected third-quarter results after the bell on Wednesday, even as automotive revenue dropped. The stock was litt
body: watch nowTesla reported better-than-expected third-quarter results after the bell on Wednesday, even as automotive revenue dropped. The stock was little changed in extended trading.Here's how the company did, compared with estimates from analysts polled by LSEG:Earnings per share: 48 cents adjusted vs. 43 cents estimatedRevenue: $28.05 billion vs. $27.9 billion estimatedTesla's earnings report lands a day after CEO Elon Musk told investors on SpaceX's quarterly call that it would be a "good idea" for his two companies to merge, and said the boards at both have formed special committees to discuss a possible tie-up."I feel like I'm tap dancing through a minefield," Musk said on the call, responding to a question about a potential merger."Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said. "But at the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this." On the Tesla side, that means needing a 50% vote of all shares, which is "quite a high hurdle," he said.Musk addressed the matter in his opening comments on the Tesla call, but didn't provide any additional information."I think I said everything that should be said yesterday," Musk said.Tesla's revenue was down slightly flat from a year earlier, when the company generated sales of $28.24 billion, Tesla said in its earnings deck. In Tesla's core automotive business, revenue declined 3% from a year earlier to $20.56 billion in the quarter. Energy revenue fell 16% to $2.88 billion.Balancing out the declines were gains in Tesla's services and other revenue. Sales there climbed 33% from a year ago to $4.61 billion. Tesla blamed its lackluster automotive revenue and profits on lower average sales prices for its cars during the quarter, and trouble securing battery supplies to make enough vehicles to fulfill a backlog of orders.Net income attributable to common share holders plummeted 29% to $787 million, or 22 cents a share, from $1.11 billion, or 32 cents a year earlier, Tesla said. The drop in profitability reflects a surge in spending on Optimus humanoid robots and other artificial intelligence initiatives. Capital expenditures more than doubled from a year earlier to $3.73 billion. Free cash flow plunged by 62% year over year to $1.53 billion, after Tesla turned free cash flow negative in the second quarter.A Tesla Bot, also known as Optimus, is displayed beside Tesla logos at a promotional exhibition in a shopping mall on September 18, 2026, in Hong Kong, China. Cheng Xin | Getty ImagesTesla said uptake of its FSD (Supervised), a partially automated driving system the company sells for $99 per month in the U.S., grew by 20 percentage points from the second quarter. Active FSD subscriptions increased 67% from a year earlier to 1.74 million."We believe that FSD is driving demand in markets where it is available, and we continue to work with regulators to get it approved in other markets," the company said in its investor deck.Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla's vice president of Autopilot, said on the earnings call that the company plans to give some customer cars access to FSD (Unsupervised) around the second quarter of next year.Tesla is testing its Cybercab, a bronze two-seater designed for use as a robotaxi, but that's not yet sold to individuals. Musk said on the call that "the vast majority of the Cybercab stuff will be essentially Tesla-owned and transport-as-a-service." The company plans to bring Cybercab in cities beyond Austin, Texas, this year, Taneja said, paying attention to operating costs like maintenance, charging and cleaning. In response to a question on the call, Musk said the Robotaxi fleet, which includes Cybercabs, will start to contribute to the company's financials in 2027. "It's not like going to move the needle this quarter," Musk said, "I think it starts to become noticeable in Q2 and then probably a big deal by Q3 or Q4 of next year."Barring regulatory intervention and protectionism, "Tesla will end up doing a majority of all passenger miles on Earth in any country where it is allowed to operate freely."Tesla said its auto sales in Canada, Japan, Taiwan and Australia hit new records during the quarter. However, the company has gotten meager growth out of its core market of late as Chinese EV makers such as BYD and Xiaomi gained popularity in Asia and Europe with affordable and innovative EVs. Tesla was also hit last year by the end of a federal EV tax credit.Earlier this month, Tesla reported vehicle deliveries for the third quarter of 486,532, about 2% below the year-ago number. Deliveries are the closest approximation of sales reported by Tesla but are not precisely defined in its shareholder communications.One of Tesla's big investments is in a semiconductor factory that it's building with SpaceX and Intel in Grimes County, Texas. That partnership with SpaceX along with other areas of overlap, including work on Tesla's recently announced Roadster refresh, fueled intensifying speculation that Musk's companies were on the verge of combining in what would be a historic transaction.On Optimus, Musk said Tesla is "making good progress" on the AI systems that control the robots in development. He said there's "still quite a lot of work to do with regard to the AI and the robot for it to be truly useful for open-ended tasks." Musk said he expects current issues around electromechanical design, reliability, usage duration, and AI to be "solved around the end of next year."WATCH: Tesla and SpaceX form special committees watch now

title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion penalty in New Mexico Cambridge Analytica case
description: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg attends the annual Allen and Co. Sun Valley Media and Technology Conference at the Sun Valley Resort in Sun Valley, Idaho, U.
body: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg attends the annual Allen and Co. Sun Valley Media and Technology Conference at the Sun Valley Resort in Sun Valley, Idaho, U.S., July 9, 2026. Brendan McDermid | ReutersMeta was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties by a New Mexico court on Wednesday as part of a data privacy case that stemmed from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago. The penalty, revealed in a court filing, comes after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse found in September the social media giant liable for misleading state citizens about how it safeguards and collects user data and prevents harmful information from flourishing on its services. Although the jury concluded that Meta had more than 43 million violations of the state's unfair practices act, with each transgression carrying a civil penalty as high as $5,000, a New Mexico judge was responsible for determining the ultimate fine. The Wednesday filing showed that the state was awarded $219.5 billion, but the penalty was ultimately reduced to $25 billion."The extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, the size of New Mexico audiences reached, and the clear intentional and systematic nature of Facebook's repeated misstatements established in the trial record support the highest level of penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act - $5,000 per violation found by the jury," New Mexico District Court Judge Francis Mathew wrote in the filing.The judge added that interest on the penalty shall accrue at the rate of 15% each year until the fine is paid off in full."For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," said New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez in a statement.He added that "this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences."Meta chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney criticized the penalty, saying in a statement that the company is "confident" that it will "prevail on appeal.""This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said in the statement. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online."Read more CNBC tech newsMeta earnings updates: AI spending, ad revenue and stock reactionTesla beats on earnings and sales even as auto revenue declinesIntel hits construction milestone at Ohio chip fab that's at least 5 years behind scheduleInvestors are questioning neoclouds' business model but Nebius says AI computing prices are risingMeta previously resolved various Cambridge Analytica-derived data privacy lawsuits across the nation as part of an overarching August settlement of nearly $17 billion with a coalition of state attorneys general in a separate federal case related to child safety and mental health. But because New Mexico was not part of the settlement, the state's data privacy case that arose from Meta's Cambridge Analytica scandal proceeded to trial in September.In 2022, the social media giant agreed to pay $725 million to settle a class action lawsuit that also sprang from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal that kicked off in 2018. That scandal rocked the Mark Zuckerberg-led company before its official name change to Meta, and focused on allegations that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica improperly accessed the information of 87 million users, raising questions about Facebook's data handling practices. Mathew said in the filing that "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations. "Pressure from senior executives to keep costs down, lack of adequate enforcement resources, inadequate investigative techniques, and a desire not to create precedent for future investigations," all contributed to what the judge characterized as a "willfully ineffective" internal examination by Facebook, the filing said.  Former New Mexico Attorney General Hector Balderas originally filed the state's Cambridge Analytica-related lawsuit in 2021, while current AG Torrez oversaw the related trial. Torrez also led his state's child safety-related trial against Meta that resulted in a March jury ruling that the social media company should pay $375 million for violating the state's unfair practices act. A New Mexico judge would later order Meta to pay $567 million into an abatement fund as part of a second phase of the case that determined the social media firm's actions created a public nuisance.  Meta said it disagreed with that New Mexico ruling and planned to appeal.WATCH: AI oversight is the topic of discourse in Washington.watch now

title: CoreWeave’s market confidence erodes as bond yields spike and stock sinks
description: CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator appears after the company's initial public offering at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York on March 28, 2025.Michael Nagl
body: CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator appears after the company's initial public offering at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York on March 28, 2025.Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesCoreWeave is facing a crisis of confidence on Wall Street that's playing out in real time among equity and bond investors. With interest rates spiking and AI build-out concerns mounting, debt-heavy neoclouds like CoreWeave are being viewed by many market participants as the most vulnerable trade in the artificial intelligence space."Sentiment is decidedly negative," Andrew Keches, a credit analyst at Barclays, wrote in a note to clients on Tuesday, referring broadly to corporate debt in tech. Keches highlighted the "speed at which AI vibes are shifting on a day-to-day basis." CoreWeave, which went public in March of last year and reached a peak market cap of about $90 billion three months later, is now valued at roughly $34 billion, with its stock down 29% this month. Its unsecured debt, meanwhile, is sporting a yield of about 15%. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconCoreWeave's stock move this monthThe spread on CoreWeave's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, is up 164% in the past year and 30% in October. It last stood at nearly 1,067 basis points, or 10.67%.CoreWeave declined to comment.The story is playing out across the neocloud sector. Shares of Nebius are down 27% this month, while IREN's stock is down 32%. In Australia, shares of data center operator NextDC plunged 40% on Wednesday after the company slashed its annual earnings forecast. Earlier this month, Australian data center company Firmus scrapped its planned initial public offering, citing market volatility and conditions. U.K. neocloud Nscale is now under the microscope as investors wait to see whether the Nvidia-backed company will go through with its IPO. The company filed to go public on the New York Stock Exchange last month. A representative from Nscale declined to comment. On hold until midtermsCoreWeave is the biggest of the pack, and is intimately tied to the U.S. AI market. Nvidia is its top institutional investor, with a stake of about 9%, according to FactSet. And more than two-thirds of CoreWeave's revenue last year came from Microsoft. That's put a spotlight on CoreWeave's financials and its ability to remain viable. The company has about $20.7 billion in debt coming due through 2030 and another $14.9 billion thereafter, with the prospects of higher interest rates on future financing.Sources on credit desks told CNBC that the high-yield debt market is effectively on hold until after the midterm elections in two weeks given ongoing concerns about the political pushback that data centers are facing. One source, who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the matter, said fixed income investors "want permitting and regulatory requirements to be substantially resolved" before they commit financing. "Given recent turbulence, pausing makes sense," Seth Meyer, global head of client portfolio management at Janus Henderson, said in an interview. watch nowCoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator, who co-founded the company in 2017 initially as a crypto-mining venture, sent a memo to employees on Thursday, which CNBC obtained, to try and tamp down concern. Intrator stressed that the company maintains a range of funding options."Our financing model combines infrastructure-backed borrowing, corporate debt, equity, and customer prepayments," Intrator wrote. He added that the company has "additional flexibility to raise equity over time as market conditions and our capital needs warrant."CoreWeave had $5.5 billion of cash and equivalents at the end of the second quarter. The company is expected to report third-quarter results next month. Analysts expect negative free cash flow in the period to swell to $10.1 billion, the highest since the company started reporting quarterly financials, according to FactSet. One issue being debated heading into the report is how much more capital CoreWeave needs to raise. Rob Oliver, a software analyst at Baird, is estimating roughly $30 billion in 2027. "Earnings may address financing measures to shore up confidence," Oliver said in an interview. "But they wouldn't need that capital until the first quarter."Another question is whether Nvidia will step in if necessary?Nvidia, which supplies the graphics processing units that CoreWeave rents out, invested $2 billion in January for a 10% stake. The purchase price was $87.20 a share. The stock is now trading at $61.82 even after jumping 6% the day of the announcement. While Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said last week that CoreWeave doesn't need a backstop, some investors say the chip giant's further participation may be necessary if credit conditions continue to worsen. Nvidia didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. Analysts at Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan Chase and Barclays have put out bullish notes on the company this week, highlighting the company's GPU-backed loans and its solid list of investment-grade customers like Microsoft and Meta. Goldman analysts emphasized the company's strength in the market relative to many of its neocloud competitors. "Not all neoclouds are created equal," they wrote, in upgrading their rating to buy from hold. "CoreWeave is likely in the top quartile of neoclouds, if not the top decile, when measured on performance and ability to execute."— CNBC's Michelle Fox and Jordan Novet contributed to this report.WATCH: Market rotation favors quality over AI leverage, says Charles Schwab's Liz Ann Sonderswatch now

title: Intel hits construction milestone at Ohio chip fab that’s at least 5 years behind schedule
description: Intel announced on Oct. 21, 2026, that crews have installed the first major structural truss at its new chip fabrication plant in New Albany, Ohio.Cou
body: Intel announced on Oct. 21, 2026, that crews have installed the first major structural truss at its new chip fabrication plant in New Albany, Ohio.Courtesy: IntelIntel has hit a milestone in the construction of its massive chip fabrication plant in New Albany, Ohio, that's running at least five years behind schedule, a delay that's coincided with soaring demand for advanced chips. On Wednesday, Intel announced that crews have installed the first major structural truss in Ohio, which means the next part of the construction has finally begun. "This represents another significant step toward expanded U.S. leading-edge semiconductor capacity," Intel Foundry head Naga Chandrasekaran wrote in a post on the company's website on Wednesday. Intel still needs customers to make the investment pay off.In September, reports surfaced that the world's leading maker of high-bandwidth memory, SK Hynix, could team up with Intel in Ohio to lease some foundry space to make memory chips at the new site. Neither company would confirm any plans.When Intel first announced the Ohio factory in 2022, it was expected to start delivering chips in 2025. Intel pushed back that timeline, now aiming to finish construction in 2030. A second Ohio fab is also planned for completion in 2031 at the site, just northeast of Columbus.The delay reflects a broader recalibration of Intel's foundry ambitions under CEO Lip-Bu Tan.The Ohio factory is only one piece of Intel's ambitious build-out to start making chips for outside customers that began under former CEO Pat Gelsinger. When Tan took the helm in 2025, his turnaround strategy was more cautious, choosing to wait for customer demand before forging ahead with ambitious chip fab plans.Still, by late 2025, Intel was in high-volume production at its Arizona chip fab, producing its most advanced 18A chips. On Wednesday, Chandrasekaran also announced that operations at its next fab in Arizona are expected to begin by the end of 2028.But Intel has yet to land a major external customer for those 18A chips coming out of Arizona. Instead, Intel is using them to make its own processors for devices.Once a dominant force in the chip manufacturing landscape, Intel hit major delays with its 7- and 10-nanometer nodes, triggering the stock's worst year ever in 2024. Customers have been reluctant to commit again since.Now, Intel's window of opportunity may have arrived alongside record demand for AI, as leading chip manufacturer Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. can't make chips fast enough. Even for the biggest chipmakers like  Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices, Apple and Broadcom,  "competition is extremely fierce," to get space on TSMC's factory lines, according to Mizuho Securities analyst Jordan Klein.Intel could offer customers an alternative source for chip production, according to TechInsights analyst Dan Hutcheson."People want a second source to be able to twist TSMC's arm and keep them honest on pricing," Hutcheson said. "All the big ones have been testing there."WATCH: Inside Intel’s new Arizona fab, where the chipmaker’s fate hangs in the balancewatch now

title: SpaceX stock jumps 10% after earnings beat and Musk hints at Tesla tie-up
description: watch nowSpaceX stock jumped 10% Wednesday after the company reported surging revenue growth in its third quarter, and owner Elon Musk floated a poten
body: watch nowSpaceX stock jumped 10% Wednesday after the company reported surging revenue growth in its third quarter, and owner Elon Musk floated a potential SpaceX-Tesla merger. The space company, which made its debut on the Nasdaq in the biggest initial public offering ever in June, reported third-quarter revenue on Tuesday of $14.6 billion, up 161% from the previous year, and beating LSEG consensus estimates of $12.72 billion. Meanwhile, its operating income came in at $2.8 billion, with net income of $4.4 billion, after reporting a net loss of $1.05 billion in the same period a year earlier. On an earnings call, Musk said he's considering a combination with Tesla — which would mark the largest merger in history — and that the boards of both companies have created specific committees to discuss a consolidation. "I do think there's a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there's a lot to be gained from cooperating," Musk said on the call. Tesla is set to report third-quarter earnings after the closing bell on Wednesday. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconSpaceX shares since its debut on the Nasdaq. Shares of other space stocks, including Rocket Lab, Intuitive Machines and AST SpaceMobile climbed on Wednesday.SpaceX forecasts first-quarter 2027 revenue between $33 billion and $37 billion, beating the average analyst estimate of $22.2 billion, according to LSEG. "We delivered another strong quarter in Q3. Revenue grew an impressive 161% year-over-year, fueled by continued momentum in Connectivity and a clear inflection in our Super Intelligence business," SpaceX's chief financial officer, Bret Johnsen, said in the earnings release. Johnsen pinned the strong results on recurring revenue from its satellite internet business, Starlink, and significant expansion of its Super Intelligence [SI] infrastructure. The company has dived into artificial intelligence this year, which it's now calling SI. The segment is its largest business unit, with revenue soaring ninefold to $7.56 billion from $813 million in the same quarter last year. watch nowBull case for AI cloud providersCommentary on computing during the earnings call supported "continued pricing power and shorter payback periods" for AI cloud providers, Truist Securities analysts said in a Tuesday note. "Despite market concerns relating to financing for AI cloud providers this past week, we believe SpaceX's third-quarter 2026 represents the first data point during the earnings season to support the bull case for AI cloud providers," they added.They explained that demand appears "insatiable," with SpaceX noting that it could rent out its capacity several times over. The analysts said Coreweave and Nebius are set to benefit and capture demand as "pricing power will more than offset higher rates."The shares of neoclouds Nebius and Coreweave traded marginally lower, while Iren and Applied Digital climbed in early trading on Wednesday.— CNBC's Lora Kolodny contributed to this report.Correction: Bret Johnsen is chief financial officer at SpaceX. An earlier version misspelled his name.Read more CNBC tech newsMeta earnings updates: AI spending, ad revenue and stock reactionTesla beats on earnings and sales even as auto revenue declinesIntel hits construction milestone at Ohio chip fab that's at least 5 years behind scheduleInvestors are questioning neoclouds' business model but Nebius says AI computing prices are rising

title: Nvidia announces plug and play Vera Rubin racks that can be shipped on a truck
description: Jensen Huang, chief executive officer of Nvidia Corp., shows Vera Rubin computer modules during the keynote address at the Nvidia GTC in Berlin, Germa
body: Jensen Huang, chief executive officer of Nvidia Corp., shows Vera Rubin computer modules during the keynote address at the Nvidia GTC in Berlin, Germany, on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. Alex Kraus | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesNvidia announced Wednesday a new product that will put seven of its Vera Rubin AI racks into a shipping container, the company's latest effort to move up the stack and offer complete systems for artificial intelligence computing.The DSX Pod AI Factory is roughly the size of a standard shipping container and weighs about 28,000 kilograms (nearly 62,000 pounds), Nvidia said. It's designed to be shipped on a truck on normal roads and all the cabling and liquid cooling for the Pod are assembled at the factory, the company said. "The only thing that has to happen when it gets to the site is it's placed in its location, connected to the rest of the other containers, and validated through final burning and testing," Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale computing at Nvidia, said on a call with reporters this week. The DSX Pod AI factory will reduce the time for a new AI data center to start serving tokens from six months to 14 days, according to the company. Nvidia said the pod is intended for customers worldwide and could help address deployment challenges faced by European customers.Nvidia did not announce a price for the system, but analysts say a single Vera Rubin rack can cost more than $7 million. The DSX Pod is a reference design that will ship from Nvidia's manufacturing partners. Nvidia said it was working with manufacturers including Foxconn, Gigabyte, Lenovo, HPE, Quanta and Pegatron. Nvidia expects deliveries to start in early 2027. Nvidia, once a chip company, now offers networking, storage and other data center needs to its customers. Its AI systems have evolved from single graphics processing unit chips to servers with four or eight GPUs, then to entire racks and now to the DSX Pod, a containerized building block with several racks already integrated. "What we offer into one gigawatt went from about $18 billion or so per gigawatt, to $20-something billion per gigawatt, to now $40-plus billion per gigawatt," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said recently on a podcast. Gigawatts refer to the size of data center infrastructure by how much power is used. "My sense is that's going to keep going up."Read more CNBC tech newsMeta earnings updates: AI spending, ad revenue and stock reactionTesla beats on earnings and sales even as auto revenue declinesIntel hits construction milestone at Ohio chip fab that's at least 5 years behind scheduleInvestors are questioning neoclouds' business model but Nebius says AI computing prices are rising

title: New Mexico AG lawsuit accuses Epstein's attorney and accountant of facilitating sex trafficking
description: Julia Molchanova, left, Anouska De Georgiou, center, and New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez speak at a news conference where Torrez announced a l
body: Julia Molchanova, left, Anouska De Georgiou, center, and New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez speak at a news conference where Torrez announced a lawsuit against the co-executors of Jeffrey Epstein's estate, Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026, in Albuquerque, N.M.Susan Montoya Bryan | APNew Mexico's attorney general on Wednesday filed a federal lawsuit accusing Jeffrey Epstein's long-time personal lawyer and accountant of facilitating Epstein's sex trafficking operation.The civil suit alleges the attorney, Darren Indyke, and the accountant, Richard Kahn, helped finance and conceal Epstein's sex trafficking, which included the abuse of girls and young women at his Zorro Ranch in Santa Fe County, New Mexico.Indyke and Kahn are beneficiaries of Epstein's 1953 Trust, co-executors of Epstein's estate, and administrators of the revocable trust, whose name comes from the year of the convicted sex offender's birth. New Mexico's suit asks a judge to block Indyke and Kahn from receiving payments from the estate as the case proceeds in U.S. District Court in New Mexico. The suit alleges the two men participated in a sex trafficking venture in violation of the federal Trafficking Victims Protection Act; and that they violated New Mexico's Racketeering Act by engaging in kidnapping, criminal solicitation and conspiracy.Darren K. Indyke, Jeffrey Epstein's former lawyer, arrives for his deposition before the House Oversight Committee on Capitol Hill, Thursday, March 19, 2026, in Washington.Jose Luis Magana | APAttorney General Raul Torrez's office said Epstein's estate is currently valued at more than $107 million, and the suit says Indyke and Kahn are eligible for bequests of $50 million and $25 million, subject to the availability of funds."Jeffrey Epstein did not operate alone, and his death does not end the pursuit of accountability for the people who helped make his crimes possible," Torrez said in a statement, which was released as he appeared at a press conference flanked by two survivors of abuse by Epstein, Anouska De Georgiou and Julia Molchanova."The allegations in this lawsuit describe a network of people and financial arrangements that helped sustain and conceal the abuse of vulnerable girls and young women, including here in New Mexico," Torrez said. "Those who allegedly enabled this exploitation should not be allowed to profit from it while survivors continue to live with its consequences."The suit comes a month after The Wall Street Journal reported that the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York had opened an investigation into Indyke and Kahn.De Georgiou said at the press conference that her abuse by Epstein and his accomplice, Ghislaine Maxwell, "did not happen in isolation.""It could not have continued for as long as it did without people facilitating it, looking the other way, or choosing to do nothing to stop it," De Georgiou said. "Accountability cannot end with Epstein and Maxwell. It must extend to those who knowingly made their abuse possible, especially those who stand to profit from it. That includes anyone who knowingly helped make Epstein appear legitimate to conceal his abuse of women and girls."Zorro Ranch, Jeffrey Epstein's New Mexico property.Courtesy: U.S. District Court of New Mexico | State of New Mexico v. Darren Indyke | Richard KahnDaniel Weiner, an attorney for Epstein's estate, in a statement to CNBC, said, "Both Mr. Indyke and Mr. Kahn reject as categorically false the allegations that they knowingly facilitated or assisted Mr. Epstein in his sexual abuse or trafficking of women, or that they were aware of Mr. Epstein's actions while they provided legal or accounting services to him.""They are confident that they will prevail on the claims asserted against them," Weiner said."Neither the New Mexico Attorney General nor anyone from his office asked to speak with Mr. Indyke or Mr. Kahn to seek relevant information from them before filing this baseless lawsuit, raising serious questions about the thoroughness of the Attorney General's investigation and the motivations for his lawsuit," Weiner said. "Messrs. Indyke and Kahn have given multiple depositions in civil lawsuits and have testified at length before the U.S. House of Representatives Committee on Oversight and Government Reform," the attorney said. "Had the New Mexico Attorney General wanted to learn the actual facts of their professional services for Epstein, the Attorney General or his staff could have reached out to schedule interviews.  Messrs. Indyke and Kahn have cooperated with any and all investigations when asked to do so."Richard Kahn, an accountant for convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, arrives for a House Oversight Committee deposition about Epstein on Capitol Hill on Wednesday, March 11, 2026.Tom Williams | Cq-roll Call, Inc. | Getty ImagesThe lawsuit alleges Indyke and Kahn personally profited from their relationship to Epstein, who killed himself in a federal jail in New York in August 2019, weeks after being arrested on child sex trafficking charges."Between 2011 and 2019, Indyke received more than $16 million from Epstein and related entities, and Kahn received more than $10 million," Torrez's office said in a statement. Torrez, at a press conference Wednesday, said his office is continuing a criminal investigation of Epstein's sex trafficking operation. No criminal charges have been filed in connection with that probe.Epstein's estate in February agreed to pay out as much as $35 million to settle a class action lawsuit in U.S. District Court in Manhattan that accused Indyke and Kahn of aiding and abetting Epstein's sex trafficking.The proposed settlement does not include any admission of misconduct by Indyke or Kahn. The judge handling the case last month endorsed a proposal by the suit's plaintiff to notify potential class members to submit claims on the settlement by conducting a four-week-long social media campaign on Facebook and Instagram.

title: Trump denies ordering Starlink slowdown in Ukraine, says he doesn't know who did
description: watch nowPresident Donald Trump on Wednesday insisted he had nothing to do with a slowdown of SpaceX's Starlink in Ukraine and said he does not know i
body: watch nowPresident Donald Trump on Wednesday insisted he had nothing to do with a slowdown of SpaceX's Starlink in Ukraine and said he does not know if Elon Musk was responsible for speed-capping the critical satellite service.Trump's latest denial came one day after The Wall Street Journal, citing unnamed U.S. officials and people familiar with the matter, reported Musk ordered the slowdown and discussed it with Trump."I wasn't involved," Trump told a reporter when asked about the decision as he departed the White House for a campaign rally in South Carolina.When pressed to answer if Musk, SpaceX's founder and CEO, ordered the slowdown, Trump said, "I don't know who did it, but I was not involved."The recent disruption of Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink, rendered some Ukrainian drones effectively useless, weakening defenses against Russian attacks.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Monday said his military still faces "speed restrictions on Starlink and Starshield services in different parts of the front.""No explanation for either of these issues has been provided to Ukraine by the American side," he said.The Journal reported Tuesday that Musk and Trump discussed the move to throttle Starlink "soon after" the change first became public last week, citing two people familiar with the matter.One of the people who spoke with the news outlet claimed Musk discussed the matter with multiple senior administration officials, including Trump himself, prior to imposing the Starlink speed cap.Trump and Musk have both recently ramped up their criticism of Zelenskyy. But neither of them has yet identified who ordered the Starlink disruption.Musk said on X last week that Starshield systems are "owned and controlled by the US government" and that any speed or usage limits are "decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS." Earlier Wednesday, Zelesnkyy said he and Norwegian Defense Minister Tore Sandvik "discussed in detail launching work on new satellite communication capabilities for our warriors.""We will involve partners who have the capacity to provide support," Zelenskyy said in an X post.Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday morning that he does not believe Musk would throttle Starlink without "at least the acquiescence of the White House."watch now

title: A $50 sports bet costs a young investor hundreds later. Here's how
description: Fstop123 | Istock | Getty ImagesFootball season is here. It's a great time for some financial wisdom. On any given fall Sunday, a 25-year-old can watc
body: Fstop123 | Istock | Getty ImagesFootball season is here. It's a great time for some financial wisdom. On any given fall Sunday, a 25-year-old can watch the early game from her couch and put $50 on a parlay from her phone before kickoff. While exciting entertainment in the short term, it comes at a potentially large long-term cost that is still underappreciated by many: compounded returns.    According to a survey of 1,000 U.S. retail investors that Betterment published in August, 52% of Gen Z investors this past year took money they had set aside for investing and put it toward sports betting instead. About a quarter said they now treat betting as part of their long-term financial strategy. Yet data from the Bank of America Institute shows just how that is going, with bettors getting back less than 75 cents on average for every dollar they sent in this year, and Gen Z, the best gambling performers of any generation, still getting back only about 80 cents in July. It's easy to understand the appeal, since a winning bet can look like a shortcut when rent is high and a first home feels out of reach. Plenty of people bet for fun, and betting out of an entertainment budget is a personal choice. The trouble comes when the money is taken from savings or money set aside to invest. A recent National Bureau of Economic Research study found that in states that legalized sports betting, household savings fell, as bets that lose money on average crowded out investments that grow, and the hit was biggest for households that could least afford it.Most young bettors don't realize that the $50 they lose on an app is the smallest part of the cost, because that $50 never gets the chance to compound, and invested at 7% a year from age 25, it would be worth about $750 at 65.  Every bet made with investment money takes from her future, and that cost never shows up on the app.That hidden cost is compounding, probably the most important idea in investing, and the one most people never learn. Compounding simply means your investment returns get reinvested and start earning returns of their own, and over time compounding is the force that turns small, regular sums into real wealth.  In our new book, "Investment Wisdom for Our Friends and Loved Ones," my co-author, Jenny Harrington, provided a simple example. A house worth $100,000 increases in value over a year by 10%, to $110,000. Then that house value, now at $110,000, rises another 10% to $121,000. That means that second year adds $11,000 rather than $10,000 because the gain was earned on a bigger base. Over decades, those returns on past returns become the largest source of growth in a portfolio, which is why the 25 women co-authors for this book, who spent their careers in finance, kept coming back to compounding as key.  Start earlyLet's go back to our young sports fan. Say she bets $50 every week, or about $2,600 a year.  If she put that money into a low-cost stock index fund earning 7%  a year, she would have roughly $519,000 by age 65 on contributions of about $104,000.  In her last year alone, the account would have grown by around $34,000 on its own.  If she did as well as the average Gen Z sports bettor instead, she would lose roughly $500 a year and have nothing working for her at 65.This brings us to the second most important part of compounding, which is that starting early matters even more than the amount. If she invested $50 a week for only ten years and then stopped, she would still have about $273,000 at 65, more than a friend who started at 35 and invested every week for 30 years, ending with about $246,000 despite putting in three times as much.  Source: Author calculations. $50 a week ($2,600 a year) added at the end of each year, 7% annual return, before fees and taxes.The first years of a working life are an investor's most valuable, and they are the years the betting apps compete for the hardest.Skipping the betting apps, or at least thoughtfully budgeting for them as entertainment, is only part of it, because money left sitting in savings accounts also misses out on compounding. Spending most of my career in bond and money markets, one learns how large that gap is. Since 1900, U.S. Treasury bills, the closest thing to cash in the bank, have returned about 3.4% a year, compared with about 9.8% for U.S. stocks, according to the UBS Global Investment Returns Yearbook. After inflation, that works out to be about 0.5% a year for bills and 6.6% for stocks. An emergency fund is essential and bonds have an important place in a portfolio, but money meant for the long run belongs in investments, which is why our book encourages parents to help teenagers open a Roth IRA with their first paychecks and invest it, so a few hundred dollars from a summer job can compound tax-free for decades.Investing strategyCosts compound too. Sara Devereux, global head of Vanguard's Fixed Income Group, shows in her chapter that on $100,000 earning 7% a year for 30 years, a fund charging 1.5% in annual fees leaves about $499,000, while one charging 0.05% leaves about $752,000. Betting is the extreme version of the same problem, since the house takes a cut on every wager and the more often you play, the more reliably the math works against you.The hardest part is leaving the money alone, because markets do fall, and the S&P 500 has lost money in roughly one of every four years since 1928. I was at the U.S. Treasury Department in 2008, when the S&P 500 Index fell 37% and the financial system came close to breaking.  While the index did not get back to its 2007 peak until March 2013 , an investor who held an S&P 500 index fund from the start of 2008 through 2025, with dividends reinvested, still ended up with more than six times her money.   None of this requires expertise or a lot of money.  Set up an automatic contribution from each paycheck, even $50 a week, choose a low-cost index fund, reinvest the dividends and leave it alone, and if you have young people in your life, talk to them about this before the betting apps do. Football season is great – enjoy it while you let your money work for you, instead of against you.Jamie Franco is a global macro and cross-asset strategist who spent over a decade at TCW Group. "Investment Wisdom for our Friends and Loved Ones" publishes Nov. 17— With Rebecca Patterson.
